summary:
Puducherry is a union territory of India with a partial legislature. Legal recognition of gender identity, identity-document rules and welfare policy for transgender people are set principally by the central government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern has been sourced. A trans visitor in Puducherry therefore stands under India's national framework rather than under any local instrument.

That framework changed in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification and narrowing the statutory definition of transgender person. Legal recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, and identity recognition is made conditional on medical certification. Both houses approved the bill and it awaits presidential assent.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, describes the amendment as a major reversal of the rights the Supreme Court affirmed in its 2014 third-gender ruling and has urged the president not to sign it. Critics characterise the mandatory medical examination as an attack on privacy and dignity. The government's stated case is that the narrower definition improves the delivery of welfare schemes.

The practical consequence for a visitor is that recognition turns on group membership and a medical certificate rather than on self-declaration. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the accepted categories fall outside the recognition scheme altogether, and rights campaigners including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. India has an estimated two million transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
India's baseline on entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to employment. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences the old law carried, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by that force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine conversion-therapy networks that continue to operate.

Facilities and care are largely organised below national level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
localsOnly:
Residents of Puducherry draw welfare provision from the national schemes rather than from any territorially specific transgender statute on file. The Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 extends transition-related healthcare to members of the transgender community as a class.

Transgender welfare boards operating in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions for residents, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits to hijras. Residents of Puducherry neighbouring those states sit alongside a patchwork of entitlements that varies by where they are resident rather than a single territorial benefit set.

Since August 2024 the Ministry of Finance has confirmed that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries, a point that applies to resident couples registering financial ties.

Protection for intersex infants in the neighbouring state of Tamil Nadu rests on the Madras High Court order of April 2019 banning sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants; no equivalent territorial order for Puducherry has been sourced.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill is unresolved in the sources on file: both houses have approved it and it awaits presidential assent, so the operative text as at the date of a visit depends on whether assent has been given.

No Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement data, incident series or court judgment on transgender recognition, documents or police conduct has been located, so claims about how the national framework is applied inside the territory rest on the national picture alone.

Whether Puducherry operates its own transgender welfare board, or administers the Ayushman Bharat transition-care expansion through territorially distinct machinery, is not sourced.

The route a trans visitor uses to obtain or present an Indian identity document under the narrowed recognition scheme, and whether the medical certification requirement applies to foreign-issued documents at entry, are not resolved by the available material.
